specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes an engineering method (Sentence Encoder) that maps arbitrary digit sequences to mnemonic sentences using the major system, POS sentence templates sampled from the Brown corpus, and a trigram language model augmented with a set of heuristics (noun-for-pronoun substitution, skipping certain POS slots, digit-weighted trigram scoring, and bigram post-processing). The authors argue that this combination yields outputs that are syntactically plausible, shorter (more digits per word), and thus more chunkable and memorable than several baselines (random, unigram, n-gram, POS-only, chunk). They evaluate output examples and run an online human-subjects study comparing sentence encodings, n-gram encodings, and raw numeric passwords for eight-digit sequences using short-term recall, long-term recall/recognition, and subjective rankings. Reported results show a short-term recall advantage and faster confirmation for sentence encodings vs n-gram, higher long-term recognition (forced-choice) and subjective preference for sentence encodings, but no long-term free-recall advantage. The paper stitches engineering choices to behavioral outcomes but lacks ablation experiments, broad quantitative coverage statistics, and some controls in the user study (notably high exclusion rate, shorter-than-intended distraction interval, and potential cueing in recognition). From a novelty lens: the work synthesizes known elements (major system, n-gram models, POS templates) into a distinct operational frame — automated sentence-based mnemonic encoding optimized for digits — which appears underexplored in the literature and could constitute a new, actionable framing for mnemonic generation despite sparse direct precedent.
logical_argument_graph: L1: Memorizing digits is hard; the major system can map digits to consonant patterns to form words (Intro & Table 1).
L2: Existing major-system tools are simplistic (single-word lists or fixed chunking) and ill-suited to generate memorable, sentence-length encodings (Section 2.1).
L3: Language-model-informed sentence structure should balance encoding completeness and syntactic plausibility, improving memorability (motivation in Intro & 3.4).

L4: Construct Sentence Encoder by sampling POS templates (from Brown), filling slots with words chosen by a trigram model, and applying heuristics to favor words that encode more digits and preserve fluency (3.4).
L5: Sentence Encoder produces shorter (fewer words, more digits per word), more chunkable outputs than baselines as shown by examples and qualitative comparison (4, 4.1).
L6: In an online user study, sentence encodings outperform n-gram encodings on short-term recall, confirmation speed, forced-choice long-term recognition, and subjective ease-of-memory (5.3).
L7: Therefore, the Sentence Encoder is a practical system-level way to generate mnemonic sentences for digit sequences that improve usability/memorability over simpler baselines (Conclusions).

identified_claims.claim_text: A Sentence Encoder that samples POS-based sentence templates (from the Brown corpus) and fills POS slots with a trigram n-gram language model (with several engineering heuristics: noun-for-pronoun substitution, POS skipping for determiners/adjectives/adverbs, digit-weighted trigram scoring (power=10), and a bigram-based post-processing pass) produces syntactically plausible sentences that encode arbitrary digit sequences using the major system.
evidence: Detailed model description in 3.4: trigram model, 100 most frequent sentence templates, POS sampling, greedy selection of words encoding digits, noun-for-pronoun substitution, POS skipping, digit-weighting (power=10), bigram post-processing.
Worked example encoding 86101521 as 'Officiate wasteland.' (3.4 and Table 2).
uncertainty_flags: Syntactic plausibility mainly argued via examples and descriptive claims; no held-out grammaticality metric or human ratings of fluency presented.
No ablation quantifying each heuristic's contribution to plausibility or encoding success rate.

identified_claims.claim_text: The Sentence Encoder generates shorter encodings (fewer words / sentences) in which each word encodes more digits (making them more chunkable and distinctive) than baseline encoders (random, unigram, n-gram, POS-only, chunk).
evidence: Examples in Tables 2 and 3: sentence encoder compresses 8-digit example into two words while other encoders produce longer sequences.
Qualitative description in 4.1 noting each word tends to encode many digits and be distinctive.
uncertainty_flags: No aggregate quantitative statistics (mean words-per-digit, distributions) shown across many inputs; claim supported primarily by illustrative examples.
Unclear how often sentence encoder produces very short vs long encodings across random inputs.

identified_claims.claim_text: In an online user study with 66 valid participants, participants assigned sentence-encoder encodings showed better short-term recall (after distraction) and faster confirmation times than participants assigned n-gram encodings.
evidence: 29/31 sentence participants (94%) vs 26/36 n-gram participants (72%) confirmed the password initially (p = 0.02, z-test).
Sentence group spent less time on confirmation page (27s vs 52s, p = 0.019, independent t-test).
uncertainty_flags: Large exclusion of responses (101 of 167 removed) may bias remaining sample; criteria and balance between groups after exclusion need scrutiny.
Distraction task was shorter than intended (median 81s vs planned 5 minutes), reducing external validity for the intended retention interval.

identified_claims.claim_text: After one week, participants recognized sentence-encoder encodings from multiple choices at higher rates than numeric passwords, and participants rated sentence-encoder encodings as easier to remember than numeric or n-gram encodings.
identified_claims.section_anchor: 5.3 Study Results - Long-Term Recognition; Subjective Comparison
evidence: Long-term recognition: 30/30 recognized sentence password vs 58/66 recognized numeric password (p = 0.05).
Subjective rankings: sentence password rated 'easiest to remember' by more participants than numeric (36/66 vs 24/66, p = 0.04), and numeric preferred to n-gram (24/66 vs 6/66, p < 0.001).
uncertainty_flags: No long-term free-recall advantage observed; recognition used forced-choice (5 options) created by same encoder family which may cue participants.
Small group sizes in long-term tests and how distractor options were generated are not fully described—possible familiarity/cueing effects.

identified_claims.claim_text: Using the intersection of the Brown corpus and the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary (~34,000 words) ensures that generated words can be pronounced and that the encoder can encode arbitrary digit sequences (coverage property).
evidence: Authors report intersecting Brown corpus and CMU dict yielding ~34k words and state encoder can encode all numbers (3.1, 3.4).
uncertainty_flags: No explicit coverage rates or failure cases across many inputs; vocabulary restriction effects on naturalness and memorability not quantified.
Some digit-to-phoneme mappings may be ambiguous for certain pronunciations or dialects (implicit assumption A5).

identified_claims.claim_text: Practical system-level choices — including sampling POS templates, weighting n-gram scores by digits encoded, POS skipping, and post-processing with bigrams — materially improve memorability and usability of generated encodings.
evidence: Sentence encoder (including these features) outperformed the n-gram encoder in short-term recall and subjective measures in the user study.
Authors report these specific heuristics as 'greatly improve' performance in 3.4.
uncertainty_flags: No controlled ablation experiments isolating each heuristic; causal links between specific heuristics and memorability outcomes are inferred by composite model comparison only.

identified_claims.claim_text: Baseline encoders (random, unigram, n-gram, POS-only, chunk) produce outputs that are less syntactically coherent, harder to chunk, and less memorable than the sentence encoder.
evidence: Qualitative descriptions in 4.1 and example tables (2 and 3) showing longer or incoherent outputs from n-gram/unigram/random baselines and computational slowness of chunk encoder.
uncertainty_flags: Comparisons rely heavily on qualitative examples; objective fluency/coherence metrics across a wide set of inputs are not provided.

strengths.title: Coherent system-level synthesis of methods
strengths.description: The paper combines POS templates, n-gram scoring, and pragmatic heuristics into a single working Sentence Encoder that operationalizes digit-to-sentence mnemonic generation.
evidence: Section 3.4 explains how trigram templates, POS sampling, digit-weighted scoring, and post-processing are combined.
Worked example and generated outputs (Tables 2 & 3) showing feasible sentences for short and long digit sequences.

strengths.title: Human-subject evaluation linking model output to behavior
strengths.description: Authors conducted an online user study comparing encodings against n-gram and raw numbers and collected multiple behavioral and subjective metrics.
evidence: Study design in Section 5 includes short-term recall, long-term recall, recognition, and subjective rankings across two surveys separated by one week.
Reported statistics (p-values) demonstrating short-term recall and confirmation-time differences.

strengths.title: Practical focus with reproducible engineering details
strengths.description: Model hyperparameters, data sources (Brown, CMU dict), and algorithmic heuristics are described in enough detail for replication and extension.
evidence: Specifics: trigram with Stupid Backoff for n-gram encoder, sampling 100 frequent templates, digit-weight power=10, post-processing using bigram scores (Sections 3.3–3.4).
Code promised to be released (Section 3. Methodology).

concerns.title: High exclusion rate in user study and possible sampling bias
concerns.description: 101 of 167 participants were excluded as 'fraudulent', leaving 66 valid participants; the exclusion criteria and potential bias introduced by removing a large chunk of data are not fully documented or sensitivity-analyzed.
evidence: 5.1 Study Overview reports 167 initial participants, 101 excluded for suspicious patterns (very short times, grouped emails, perfect recall), leaving 67 then 66.
Shared analysis notes recommending reproducing exclusion procedure and checking bias.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a precise, reproducible description of exclusion rules and thresholds, report characteristics (demographics, baseline performance) of excluded vs retained participants, and run sensitivity analyses showing whether main results hold under alternative exclusion thresholds.

concerns.title: Lack of ablation to isolate heuristic contributions
concerns.description: Multiple heuristics (POS skipping, noun substitution, digit-weighting, post-processing) were combined into the final model but no ablation study isolates which elements drive syntactic plausibility or memorability gains.
evidence: 3.4 lists four changes that 'greatly improve' performance, but Shared Analysis and text reveal no per-heuristic ablation or effect sizes.
Conclusions and chaining_notes call for targeted ablation experiments.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run controlled ablations where each heuristic is toggled, measuring fluency metrics (human ratings or automated grammaticality/perplexity) and memorability in a scaled pilot to attribute causal effects.

concerns.title: Sparse quantitative metrics for encoding length, coverage, and fluency
concerns.description: Claims about shorter encodings and superior chunkability are supported mainly by illustrative examples instead of aggregate statistics over many randomly sampled digit sequences and objective fluency measures.
evidence: 4 and 4.1 provide examples and qualitative comparisons but no mean words-per-digit, distribution of sentence lengths, or failure-case frequencies.
Coverage claim (encode all numbers) lacks empirical rates or timeouts.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute and report aggregate statistics across a large sample of random inputs: words-per-digit, sentences-per-10-digits, percent of inputs requiring template resampling, and automatic fluency proxies (perplexity, POS-sequence likelihood), plus runtime/latency measures.

concerns.title: Arbitrary tuning of digit-weighting (power=10) without justification
concerns.description: The choice to weight trigram score by (digits encoded)^(power) with power=10 is asserted to prefer words encoding more digits but no systematic search or sensitivity analysis is presented.
evidence: 3.4 describes the power parameter set to 10 with an intuition but no ablation or grid search reported.
Shared Analysis flags assumption A2 about calibration risk.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report experiments sweeping the power parameter (e.g., 0,1,2,5,10,20) and show its effect on word-length distributions, sentence naturalness, and downstream memorability (pilot or offline proxies).

concerns.title: Shorter-than-intended distraction interval reduces external validity
concerns.description: The distraction task intended to be ~5 minutes averaged 81 seconds, which weakens interpretation of the short-term recall experiment as a 5-minute retention test.
evidence: 5.1 and 6 note median distraction time 81s vs intended 5 minutes and recommend enforcing timers in future studies.
Short-term recall results are reported as if reflecting a 5-minute interval.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Re-run the short-term recall with enforced timers or report analyses stratified by actual distraction duration to assess whether group differences persist when distraction times are comparable and sufficiently long.

concerns.title: Recognition test design may cue participants and inflate effects
concerns.description: Long-term recognition used 5-option forced choice with distractors generated by the same encoder family; this design can inflate recognition rates and confound recognition advantages with familiarity of encoder style.
evidence: 5.2 and 5.3 describe recognition from five options generated by the group's encoder; Shared Analysis flags potential cueing.
Long-term free recall was not significantly different across groups while recognition differences were reported.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify how distractors were generated (random same-group outputs? carefully matched confusers?), and either use novel distractors (e.g., human-generated plausible distractors) or report recognition rates with distractors from other encoder families to test for style-familiarity effects.

concerns.title: Statistical testing choices and small group sizes
concerns.description: Some statistical tests (z-tests for proportions, t-tests for times) are used on relatively small samples after exclusion; assumptions (normality, independence, sample size) and multiple-comparisons handling are not discussed.
evidence: 5.3 reports p-values for z-tests and t-tests with group sizes as small as 30 and 36.
Shared Analysis recommends reassessing test assumptions and possibly using nonparametric/ exact tests.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report confidence intervals and effect sizes; verify test assumptions (e.g., use Fisher exact test or permutation tests for small proportions, and Wilcoxon rank-sum for non-normal timing data), and correct for multiple comparisons where applicable.

concerns.title: Vocabulary/corpus representativeness assumption
concerns.description: Using Brown∩CMU yields ~34k words, but the assumption that this vocabulary and Brown's stylistic mix generalize to target users is untested and might affect naturalness/memorability for diverse user populations.
evidence: 3.1 describes the intersection and authors state their model ensures pronouncability; Shared Analysis lists assumption A1.
No user demographic or dialiectal analyses provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report commonness/frequency statistics of generated words, test with participants from broader demographics/dialects, and consider augmenting training data (web text, more contemporary corpora) or allowing user-preferred vocabularies.

comparable_works.relevance: Close related prior work on generating memorable encodings of random bitstrings; tackles memorability but not reversible major-system digit mapping.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar goal (memorable mapping from artificial strings to words) but differs: their most memorable methods did not permit easy mental reconstruction of the original string; the present paper preserves invertibility via the major system.
comparable_works.source_trace: Shared Analysis; References: Ghazvininejad and Knight (2015)

comparable_works.relevance: Prior corpus-based mnemonic method for text passwords using headlines; demonstrates feasibility constraints when relying on fixed corpora.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Related in using corpus artifacts for mnemonic generation but limited coverage (only ~40% coverage for 7-char passwords) — contrasts with this paper's attempt at full-coverage via phonetic mapping.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 2.2; References

comparable_works.relevance: User-study design inspiration and earlier evidence that mnemonic passphrases can be memorable, informing the current experimental choices.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Provides experimental precedent for passphrase memorability; differs in encoding method and specifics of testing (this paper's forced-choice recognition and POS-based generation are new).
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 2.2 and 5.2; References

comparable_works.relevance: Findings about which sampled phrases are more memorable for text-entry experiments; informs the design choice to prefer complete phrases and moderate length.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar concern about phrase selection and memorability; this work extends these ideas into digit encoding with a generative major-system constraint.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 2.2; References

uncertainty_flags: Large participant exclusion (101/167) and sparse reporting about excluded cohort's characteristics introduce high uncertainty about sample representativeness and robustness of reported p-values.
No ablation experiments; thus attribution of memorability gains to specific heuristics is speculative.
Shorter distraction duration than intended reduces interpretability of 'short-term recall' as a 5-minute retention test.
Recognition test uses forced-choice distractors from same encoder family, potentially introducing cueing/familiarity confounds.
Claims about encoding length and coverage rely mainly on examples instead of aggregated metrics.
alternative_interpretations: Observed short-term advantage for sentence encodings could arise from increased distinctiveness or perceptual salience of particular generated words (e.g., rare/striking words) rather than from sentence structure per se.

Recognition benefit may reflect encoder-style familiarity (participants remember stylistic patterns) or cueing from distractors rather than genuinely stronger memory for the mapping between words and digits.
High exclusion of participants could have removed clusters of low-performing honest participants or systematically altered group balance, artificially boosting apparent effects.
Post-processing bigram substitutions might produce outputs that are stylistically homogeneous leading to easier forced-choice recognition but not better free recall.
transparency_notes: Model details (data sources, heuristics, example outputs) are described and code is promised, which aids reproducibility; nevertheless, hyperparameter choices (digit-weight power=10) and the exclusion algorithm need more explicit specification.
User study reports p-values and counts but lacks confidence intervals, effect sizes, and precise exclusion thresholds; raw anonymized data or analysis scripts would facilitate verification.
Several claims rely on qualitative examples; authors should supply bulk quantitative analyses and ablation code to make causal claims transparent.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The system-level framing (automated sentence generation constrained by a reversible phonetic major system) is conceptually novel relative to the retrieved literature; novelty should be treated as a signal prompting further controlled validation rather than as proof of effectiveness. Sparse precedent does not validate the empirical claims without stronger ablation and replication.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If ablations show that digit-weighted scoring and POS-template sampling independently improve chunkability and fluency, the conceptual frame is validated as a useful design pattern for mnemonic generation.
If larger, pre-registered user studies with enforced distraction intervals and non-cued recognition replicate the short-term and recognition advantages, the approach scales beyond anecdotal examples.
If vocabulary coverage statistics show low failure rates and the mapping is unambiguous across dialects, the approach can be broadly deployed for short- and medium-length password support.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper combines reversible phonetic encoding (major system) with generative sentence templates and n-gram scoring to produce mnemonic sentences — a framing that appears underexplored and could open a new line of work on generative mnemonic systems that prioritize invertibility and naturalness simultaneously.
evidence: Sparse prior art: only two corpus-based prior methods cited (news-headline mapping and bit-string mapping) that do not achieve the same combination of invertibility and sentence-level generation (Section 2.2).
Operationalized heuristics for balancing length vs fluency (digit-weighted scoring, POS template sampling) suggest a reproducible design space.
uncertainty_flags: No ablations and limited study replication reduce confidence that the conceptual frame will generalize without refinement.

novelty_lenses.rationale: From a narrow ML/NLP perspective, the components (n-gram models, POS templates, post-processing) are established techniques; novelty is in their combination and application to the major system rather than in novel algorithms or learning methods.
evidence: Use of Brown corpus n-grams, CMU dictionary, and POS templates are standard resources and methods (Sections 3.1–3.4).
Comparable works address related mapping tasks (Ghazvininejad & Knight) though without reversible major-system constraints.
uncertainty_flags: Even if incremental at the component level, the integrative application to mnemonic digit encoding may have outsized usability impact if validated.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident in the descriptive and engineering claims (model construction, example outputs). Confidence in the behavioral claims is lower due to the high exclusion rate, non-ideal distraction timing, possible recognition cueing, and absence of ablation studies; these methodological issues could materially change effect-size estimates on replication.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper presents a Sentence Encoder that generates mnemonic sentences encoding digit sequences under the major system by sampling frequent POS-based sentence templates from the Brown corpus and filling slots using a trigram language model over the Brown∩CMU vocabulary, with several heuristics (noun-for-pronoun substitution, skipping low-information POS, heavy digit-weighting of trigram scores, and bigram post-processing). The authors compare this composite model to several baselines qualitatively and with examples, and run an online user study (initial N=167; after excluding 101 suspected fraudulent responses, N=66) comparing sentence encodings, n-gram encodings, and numeric passwords on short-term recall, one-week recognition, and subjective ease. Evidence in the manuscript supports that the Sentence Encoder produces syntactically plausible, often shorter encodings in illustrative cases, and that participants assigned sentence-encoder encodings had higher short-term confirmation rates and faster confirmation times than those assigned n-gram encodings; forced-choice recognition and subjective preference measures also favor sentence encodings. However, many inferential steps are only indirectly supported: quantitative distributions (e.g., words-per-digit, coverage/failure rates) and ablation studies isolating the effect of each heuristic are absent; the human-study exclusions, unexpectedly short distraction interval, and recognition design introduce uncertainty about effect sizes and generalizability. I classify claims as supported, partially supported, or overstated below and flag where further analyses are needed to reduce uncertainty.
logical_argument_graph: Design goal: produce mnemonic encodings that (a) exactly encode digits via major system and (b) are syntactically plausible and memorable.

Implementation: train trigram on Brown, extract top 100 POS templates, restrict vocabulary to Brown∩CMU (~34k words), sample templates and greedily fill slots using digit-weighted trigram scoring, with noun-for-pronoun, POS skipping, and bigram post-processing heuristics (C1).
Model output claim: sentence encoder yields shorter, chunkable encodings (more digits per word), and more distinctive words than baselines (C2, C7).

Human evaluation claim: in an online study, sentence encodings improved short-term recall and confirmation speed vs n-gram baseline; long-term recognition and subjective preference also favorable (C3, C4).
Practical claim: engineering choices (POS templates, digit-weighting, POS skipping, post-processing) materially improve memorability/usability (C6).
Gaps: No ablations or aggregated encoding statistics to attribute improvements to specific heuristics; study exclusions and protocol deviations reduce certainty (A1-A9).

identified_claims.claim_text: A Sentence Encoder that samples POS-based sentence templates and fills POS slots with a trigram n-gram language model (with engineering heuristics: noun-for-pronoun substitution, POS skipping for determiners/adjectives/adverbs, digit-weighted trigram scoring (power=10), and a bigram-based post-processing pass) produces syntactically plausible sentences that encode arbitrary digit sequences using the major system.
evidence: Section 3.4 describes training a trigram on Brown, storing 100 most frequent sentence templates, sampling templates, and selecting words by trigram score subject to encoding constraints.
Manuscript lists the four heuristics and gives the 86101521 -> 'Officiate wasteland.' example demonstrating plausibility and encoding correctness.
uncertainty_flags: No ablation or quantitative grammaticality metric; plausibility is demonstrated via examples rather than held-out evaluation.
No systematic failure/corner-case reporting for arbitrary sequences (e.g., rare digit patterns).

identified_claims.claim_text: The Sentence Encoder generates shorter, more chunkable, and more distinctive word sequences (each word encoding more digits) than simpler baselines (random, unigram, n-gram, POS-only, chunk encoders).
evidence: Table 2 example: sentence encoder encodes 86101521 as two words while baselines produce longer outputs.
Section 4.1 states sentence encoder produces words that encode many digits and thus fewer words/sentences are needed.
uncertainty_flags: No aggregated quantitative statistics (e.g., mean words-per-digit, distribution over many inputs) provided to validate generality beyond examples.
Unclear frequency of very short encodings vs longer ones across many inputs.

identified_claims.claim_text: In an online user study with 66 valid participants, participants assigned sentence-encoder encodings showed better short-term recall (after distraction) and faster confirmation times than participants assigned n-gram encodings.
evidence: 29/31 sentence participants (94%) remembered at confirmation vs 26/36 n-gram participants (72%); reported p = 0.02 (z-test).
Sentence participants spent less time on confirmation page (27s vs 52s), p = 0.019 (t-test).
uncertainty_flags: High exclusion rate (101/167 removed) with qualitative exclusion criteria; potential selection bias in final N=66.
Distraction page median time for valid participants was 81s (less than intended 5 minutes), so the intended short-term retention interval was not met.
Statistical tests reported without diagnostics (e.g., normality for t-test) and with modest sample sizes.

identified_claims.claim_text: After one week, participants recognized sentence-encoder encodings from multiple choices at higher rates than numeric passwords, and participants rated sentence-encoder encodings as easier to remember than numeric or n-gram encodings.
identified_claims.section_anchor: 5.3 Study Results - Long-Term Recognition; Subjective Comparison
evidence: Long-term recognition: 30/30 recognized the sentence password vs 58/66 recognized the numeric password (p = 0.05).
Subjective ranking: more participants rated sentence password 'easiest' than numeric (36/66 vs 24/66, p = 0.04) and numeric rated easier than n-gram (24/66 vs 6/66, p < 0.001).
uncertainty_flags: Free long-term recall counts show no significant differences — recognition advantage does not imply free-recall superiority.
Recognition test used 5-AFC with distractors generated by same encoder family (possible cueing/familiarity bias).

identified_claims.claim_text: Using the intersection of the Brown corpus and the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary (~34,000 words) ensures that generated words can be pronounced and that the encoder can encode arbitrary digit sequences (coverage property).
evidence: Section 3.1: Brown corpus and CMU intersection yields ~34k words; Section 3.4 claims encoder can encode all numbers as plausible sentences.
uncertainty_flags: No explicit coverage statistics (e.g., failure rates, average digits-per-word across random inputs); effect of vocabulary restriction on naturalness and memorability not quantified.

identified_claims.claim_text: Practical system-level choices (POS templates, trigram scoring weighted by digits encoded, POS skipping, post-processing) materially improve the memorability and usability of generated encodings.
evidence: Authors state they combined elements from preliminary models into final model and that these changes 'greatly improve' performance; final model outperformed n-gram baseline in study.
uncertainty_flags: No ablation experiments isolating contribution of each heuristic; causal link inferred from composite model comparison only.

identified_claims.claim_text: Baseline encoders (random, unigram, n-gram, POS-only, chunk) produce outputs that are less syntactically coherent, harder to chunk, and less memorable than the sentence encoder.
evidence: Qualitative descriptions and example tables (Table 2 and 3) show longer or less coherent outputs for baselines compared to sentence encoder.
uncertainty_flags: Comparisons mostly qualitative and example-based; limited quantitative metrics of coherence/fluency or perceptual ratings before user study.

strengths.title: Clear engineering-to-cognition pipeline
strengths.description: Paper explicitly connects design choices (shorter encodings, chunkability, syntactic plausibility) to hypothesized cognitive benefits for memorability, making the reasoning easy to follow.
evidence: Sections 1, 3.4, and 4.1 articulate the link from word-level encoding density to chunkability to expected memorability.

strengths.title: Concrete reproducible system description
strengths.description: Authors give detailed implementation steps (training trigram on Brown, template selection, heuristics) and promise to release source code, supporting reproducibility.
evidence: Section 3.4 details algorithmic steps and heuristics; Section 3.1 documents data sources (Brown, CMU).
Manuscript: 'The source code for these models will be made available online.'

strengths.title: Behavioral evaluation directly tests memorability
strengths.description: The online human-subject study measures multiple memory outcomes (short-term recall, long-term recall, forced-choice recognition, subjective rankings) providing behavioral evidence.
evidence: Section 5 describes study design with two surveys, distraction task, confirmation and 1-week follow-up measuring recall and recognition.

strengths.title: Practical and plausible examples
strengths.description: Illustrative examples (8-digit and first 50 digits of π) demonstrate that the system can produce short, grammatical-looking encodings in many cases.
evidence: Tables 2 and 3 show side-by-side encodings from different models, with sentence encoder outputs like 'Officiate wasteland.'

concerns.title: Lack of ablation to attribute heuristic contributions
concerns.description: The final model bundles several heuristics (noun substitution, POS skipping, digit-weighting power=10, bigram post-processing) but no controlled ablation experiments are provided to quantify each heuristic's effect on output fluency, encoding length, or memorability.
evidence: Section 3.4 lists heuristics and asserts they 'greatly improve' performance but manuscript lacks per-heuristic comparisons or ablation results.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run and report ablation experiments: evaluate variants with each heuristic toggled off (and combinations) on (a) quantitative encoding metrics (words-per-digit distribution, sentence length distribution, LM-perplexity or grammaticality proxy) and (b) a small behavioral pilot to see which heuristics affect memorability.

concerns.title: Sparse quantitative encoding statistics
concerns.description: Claims about producing shorter and more chunkable encodings are supported mainly by illustrative examples; no aggregate statistics (mean words-per-digit, coverage/failure rates, vocabulary usage) are provided.
evidence: Section 4 gives examples but no tables/plots summarizing encoding-length distributions across a large random sample of digit sequences.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide summary statistics across a large set of random digit sequences (e.g., N=1000): words-per-digit, fraction of encodings ≤K words, distribution of digits-per-word, and failure cases where no template/word was found.

concerns.title: Human study exclusions and transparency
concerns.description: A large fraction of initial participants (101/167) were removed as 'fraudulent' with qualitative descriptions of suspicious patterns; the exclusion process may introduce bias and is not fully reproducible.
evidence: Section 5.1 describes suspicious characteristics (consecutive submissions, very short times, grouped emails) leading to exclusion but does not give exact algorithmic criteria or examine sensitivity of results to different filtering thresholds.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide precise exclusion criteria and reproducible code/filters; report study results with and without exclusions (sensitivity analysis) and describe demographic balance across treatment arms after exclusions.

concerns.title: Deviation from intended distraction interval
concerns.description: The intended 5-minute distraction task was not enforced and valid participants spent a median of 81 seconds, shorter than planned, which changes the intended retention interval for 'short-term' recall.
evidence: Section 5.1 and 6 note actual median time 81s and recommend enforcing timers in future studies.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Re-run or augment the experiment enforcing the planned distraction duration (with a timer) to test robustness of short-term recall differences; at minimum report correlations between distraction time and recall to assess bias.

concerns.title: Recognition test cueing and ecological validity
concerns.description: Long-term memory advantage is reported on 5-AFC recognition where distractors were generated by the same encoder family — forced-choice tasks can inflate memory estimates via familiarity and cueing and may not reflect free-recall performance.
evidence: Section 5.2 describes recognition as selecting from five sequences generated by the participant's group's encoder; Section 5.3 reports recognition advantage alongside non-significant free-recall differences.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify how distractors were generated and consider adding more conservative recognition tests (e.g., distractors from other encoder families and from real-world-like foils) or report recognition performance corrected for guess rate; report effect sizes for free recall vs recognition separately.

concerns.title: Statistical testing details and robustness
concerns.description: Reported p-values use z-tests and t-tests but lack diagnostics (normality checks, exact/binomial tests for small proportions) and effect size estimates; modest group sizes after exclusion may invalidate asymptotic approximations.
evidence: Section 5.3 reports p-values (e.g., p=0.02 z-test for proportions; p=0.019 t-test for time) without confidence intervals, effect sizes, or alternative nonparametric tests.
Group sizes are small (e.g., 31 vs 36) after exclusion.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report effect sizes (risk differences, odds ratios, Cohen's d), 95% CIs, and run exact/binomial tests for proportions or nonparametric tests for time; check robustness to multiple-testing if relevant.

concerns.title: Coverage and decoding ambiguity
concerns.description: The assumption that Brown∩CMU vocabulary (~34k words) provides full coverage and that users can unambiguously map words to digits via major system is asserted but not empirically validated (e.g., user decoding error rates, ambiguous pronunciations).
evidence: Section 3.1 documents the vocabulary size; Section 3.4 and discussion assert encoder can encode all numbers, but no empirical tests of human decoding accuracy for generated words are reported.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report coverage statistics over many random digit sequences and run small user tests where naive participants are asked to map generated words back to digits (measure decoding error rates), especially for infrequent words or ambiguous pronunciations.

comparable_works.relevance: Related prior work on encoding random bitstrings as memorable word sequences; shows feasibility of corpus-based mnemonic encoding but without reversible mapping to original bits.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar in using corpora to produce memorable outputs; differs because current paper enforces reversible mapping via the major system and focuses on digit sequences rather than bits.

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar motivation (corpus-based mnemonic aid) but different technique (searching headlines vs generating syntactically-plausible sentences constrained by major system).
comparable_works.source_trace: Manuscript Section 2.2 references Jeyaraman and Topkara (2005)

comparable_works.relevance: Informs human-subject study design (recall after 5 minutes and one week) and prior evidence about passphrase memorability.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Provides experimental template; current study differs in encoding method and sample construction.
comparable_works.source_trace: Manuscript Section 2.2 and references

comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Complementary prior work on phrase selection; current paper operationalizes encoding constraint (major system) and template sampling.

uncertainty_flags: High participant exclusion proportion (101/167) with qualitative criteria — possible selection bias and sensitivity of significance to exclusions.
Distraction duration was shorter than protocol (median 81s vs intended 5min) — changes interpretation of 'short-term' recall.
No ablation experiments — causal claims linking specific heuristics to memorability are speculative.
Recognition test design (5-AFC with within-encoder distractors) may inflate long-term memory estimates.
Encoding claims rely heavily on illustrative examples; lacking distributional summaries reduces generalizability confidence.
alternative_interpretations: Short-term recall advantage may stem primarily from the Sentence Encoder producing fewer and/or more distinctive words per encoding (reducing items to rehearse) rather than from improved syntactic plausibility per se; without ablation we cannot separate these mechanisms.

Recognition advantage could be due to familiarity or surface-level cues introduced by encoder-specific word choices (distractors generated similarly), inflating forced-choice performance relative to free recall.
High exclusion rate might have preferentially removed low-effort participants or particular demographic groups unevenly across treatment arms, producing artifactual group differences.
transparency_notes: Authors state source code will be released; sharing code and data (including exclusion filter code and raw study logs) is critical to reproduce the filtering and analyses.
Provide exact random seeds, template lists, and hyperparameter settings (e.g., digit-weighting power=10) to allow replication of generation and ablation.
Report full per-participant logs (time on pages, distraction time, confirmation attempts) in anonymized form to allow sensitivity analyses.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The method combines familiar components (major system, n-gram models, POS templates) but their particular orchestration for reversible, short sentence mnemonic generation appears underexplored; novelty is plausible but does not guarantee empirical robustness.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If ablation shows digit-weighting and POS templates each contribute meaningfully to reducing words-per-digit while preserving grammaticality, the approach will robustly improve memorability.
If coverage tests show near-zero failure rates across random digit sequences with acceptable average sentence lengths, the method scales to practical password lengths.
If a replication enforcing distraction duration and with transparent exclusion rules reproduces short-term recall and subjective advantages, the findings generalize to real-world password use.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The work assembles known components (major system, POS templates, n-gram language models) into a practical system with heuristics tailored to encoding digits; this is a useful engineering contribution though not a radical algorithmic innovation.
evidence: Prior corpus-based mnemonic methods exist (Ghazvininejad & Knight, Jeyaraman & Topkara); manuscript combines these elements with new operational constraints for reversible digit encoding.
uncertainty_flags: Absence of broader literature matches in retrieval corpus doesn't invalidate novelty but suggests sparse precedent; treat as moderate novelty signal.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Mapping arbitrary digit sequences to short, syntactically plausible sentences that are mentally reversible via major system could change how mnemonic password schemes are operationalized if robustness and usability are demonstrated at scale.
evidence: Demonstrated example encodings that are very concise (e.g., two-word representation of an 8-digit number) and initial behavioral evidence favoring memorability.
uncertainty_flags: Behavioral robustness and security/usability tradeoffs require more evidence (ablation, coverage, decoding error rates, scaled user studies).

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident in the paper's descriptive claims about the algorithm (implementation and example outputs) due to detailed methodological reporting (high lower bound). I am less confident in the strength and generalizability of the behavioral claims given the high exclusion rate, protocol deviations, absence of ablations, and limited quantitative encoding statistics (upper bound reflects plausible replication but substantial uncertainty).

consensus_findings: The paper presents a well-specified engineering pipeline (Sentence Encoder) that combines POS-template sampling from the Brown corpus, a trigram n-gram language model over Brown ∩ CMU vocabulary, and explicit heuristics (noun-for-pronoun substitution, POS skipping, digit-weighted trigram scoring, bigram post-processing) to generate mnemonic sentences that encode digit sequences via the major system.

Illustrative examples show the Sentence Encoder can produce compact, syntactically-plausible looking encodings (including very short encodings for some 8-digit inputs) and longer encodings for longer digit sequences (e.g., 50 digits of π).

An online human-subjects experiment is reported comparing sentence-encoder outputs, an n-gram baseline, and raw numeric passwords; reported results show higher short-term confirmation rates and faster confirmation times for the sentence-encoder group versus the n-gram baseline, and favorable forced-choice recognition and subjective preference for sentence encodings.

Major methodological gaps are identified across reviews: lack of ablation experiments isolating the contribution of each heuristic, sparse aggregate quantitative statistics about encoding length/coverage/fluency, and human-study design/execution issues (large participant exclusions, deviation from intended distraction interval, and possible cueing in recognition tests).
disagreements: Degree of confidence in behavioral claims: some reviewers view the short-term recall result as reasonably suggestive albeit needing replication (moderate confidence), while others put substantially more weight on the exclusion rate and protocol deviations and thus express low confidence in the generalizability of the reported effects.

Novelty characterization: reviewers converge that the work is an engineering synthesis of known components, but they differ on framing its novelty — some judge it a meaningful incremental contribution with practical value, whereas others view the framing as potentially disruptive if validated but caution that novelty alone does not imply practical effectiveness.

Interpretation of recognition results: some reviewers treat improved forced-choice recognition as evidence of long-term memory benefits (with caveats), while others emphasize that lack of free-recall improvements and within-encoder distractor generation make the recognition advantage plausibly driven by cueing or surface familiarity.
uncertainty_hotspots: Ablation attribution: which specific heuristics (digit-weighting magnitude, POS-skipping, noun-for-pronoun substitution, bigram post-processing, template selection) drive the observed encoding brevity and memorability is unknown because no controlled ablations were reported.

Encoding distributional statistics: aggregate rates (mean/median words-per-digit, distribution of sentence lengths, frequency of template resampling, percent of inputs requiring POS-skips), and failure/coverage rates across many random digit sequences are not provided, limiting assessment of practical performance at scale.

Human-study data quality and robustness: 101 of 167 initial participants were excluded as 'fraudulent' with qualitative descriptions but without fully reproducible filters or sensitivity analyses; this high exclusion rate is a major uncertainty about representativeness and whether results are robust to alternative inclusion rules.

Distraction interval validity: the intended ~5-minute distraction was not enforced (median observed ~81s), undermining the interpretation of 'short-term' recall results for the planned retention interval.

Recognition test validity: the 5-alternative forced-choice recognition used distractors generated by the same encoder family, introducing risk of cueing/familiarity effects that may inflate recognition-based long-term memory measures.

Statistical inference details: reliance on asymptotic z- and t-tests with modest post-exclusion group sizes without presented diagnostics, exact tests, effect sizes, or confidence intervals raises uncertainty about reported p-values' robustness.
model_diversity_effects: Combining diverse modeling choices (POS templates + n-gram LM + digit-weighting + post-processing) appears to produce qualitatively different outputs than simpler baselines: outputs tend to be shorter (fewer words), more sentence-like, and apparently more distinctive per example comparisons. This output diversity plausibly creates stronger surface cues that aid forced-choice recognition and reduce rehearsal burden for short-term confirmation, but it also confounds causal attribution (is benefit from sentence structure, from fewer words, from distinctive rare words, or from template sampling?).

The composite model design creates multiple interacting mechanisms: (a) digit-weighting increases digits-per-word and thus reduces item count; (b) POS templates impose syntactic scaffolding improving local plausibility; (c) post-processing adjusts local collocations. Different reviewers emphasize different mechanisms as primary drivers of memorability — demonstrating sensitivity to model-component variation (diversity) is needed to resolve which effects are robust versus model-artifact-driven.

The diversity of baselines evaluated (random, unigram, n-gram, POS-only, chunk) helped showcase failure modes, but only the n-gram baseline was compared in the human study. The lack of human data across multiple encoder variants limits understanding of how model diversity maps to human-memory outcomes.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Consider asking the authors to (1) provide reproducible details and sensitivity analyses for the human-subject exclusions (exact filters, per-participant timing logs, pre/post-exclusion balances) and to re-run core analyses under alternative inclusion thresholds; (2) report aggregate, corpus-scale encoding statistics (words-per-digit distribution, sentence-length distribution, coverage/failure rates across many random inputs, runtime per input for each encoder), and make generation outputs and template lists available for inspection; (3) conduct and report controlled ablation experiments that toggle each major heuristic (digit-weighting power sweep, disable POS-skipping, disable noun-for-pronoun substitution, disable post-processing) and present automatic proxies for fluency (LM scores, perplexity) plus at least a small behavioral pilot for the most important ablations; (4) clarify recognition-distractor generation methodology and, if possible, present recognition analyses with distractors not drawn from the same encoder family or report free-recall analyses separately; (5) provide statistical robustness checks (exact/binomial tests for proportions, nonparametric tests for timing, effect sizes and CIs) and correct for multiple comparisons where applicable. Position the editor as the arbiter: request these transparency and robustness items before using behavioral claims to support strong generalization.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen evidential claims and transparency, the authors should: (1) release code, template lists, and the vocabulary intersection plus seeds used to generate examples; (2) publish anonymized per-participant logs (timestamps, distraction times, confirmation attempts) and exact exclusion scripts so others can reproduce the filtering and perform sensitivity analyses; (3) add aggregate encoding statistics over large random samples (words-per-digit, fraction of encodings ≤ target word-counts, template-resampling rates, runtime per encoding) and illustrate representative failure cases; (4) run ablation experiments removing or varying key heuristics (including a sweep over the digit-weighting power parameter) and report how each affects encoding-length metrics and LM-fluency proxies; (5) clarify how recognition distractors were constructed and, if feasible, report recognition results using alternative distractors and free-recall separately; (6) report effect sizes, confidence intervals, and alternative statistical tests robust to small samples (Fisher exact, permutation tests, Wilcoxon) and present sensitivity of main inferences to inclusion/exclusion choices; (7) for future human experiments, enforce the intended distraction timing programmatically and preregister exclusion rules. These steps will clarify which engineering choices drive effects and will make behavioral claims more robust.
transparency_report: All reviewers request release of code, templates, vocabulary lists (Brown ∩ CMU), random seeds, and generation outputs used in the paper.

Authors should publish the exact fraud/exclusion filters and scripts, plus anonymized participant logs (page timestamps, page durations, responses) to permit reproduction of exclusions and sensitivity checks.

Provide the list and sampling method for the 100 POS templates, the mechanism to generate recognition distractors, and the hyperparameter settings (e.g., digit-weighting power) and any tuning procedures used.

Statistical reporting should include contingency tables, raw counts per condition, effect sizes, and confidence intervals alongside reported p-values, and indicate which tests were pre-specified vs exploratory.
epistemic_limits: The synthesis is limited by lack of access to raw data, exact exclusion code, and aggregate generation outputs; reviewers therefore reason from reported summaries, examples, and described procedures. Inferences about causality (which heuristics cause memorability gains) cannot be resolved without ablation data. The human-study evidence is constrained by possible post-hoc filtering and protocol deviation (shorter distraction) that could materially alter effect sizes; without reproducible exclusion criteria and sensitivity analyses, the external validity of behavioral findings remains uncertain. Recognize that sparse prior art in exactly this task (invertible major-system sentence generation) is a possible novelty signal but does not substitute for robustness checks; the current evidence supports feasibility and suggestive behavioral benefit but does not conclusively demonstrate which engineering components or deployment settings will reliably produce those benefits across populations and retention intervals.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript introduces a Sentence Encoder that maps digit sequences to mnemonic sentences via the major system by sampling POS-based sentence templates (from the Brown corpus) and filling slots using a trigram LM over a Brown ∩ CMU vocabulary, augmented by heuristics (noun-for-pronoun substitution, POS skipping, digit-weighted trigram scoring with power=10, and bigram post-processing). Illustrative examples show compact, sentence-like encodings; an online user study (initial N=167; after excluding 101 responses, analyzed N=66) reports higher short-term confirmation rates and faster confirmation times for sentence encodings versus an n-gram baseline, plus higher forced-choice recognition and subjective ease ratings. Reviewers agree the engineering synthesis is clear and promising but identify methodological and evidentiary gaps (lack of ablations, sparse aggregate encoding statistics, high exclusion rate and non-enforced distraction timing, and potential cueing in recognition).
strengths: Clear, reproducible engineering pipeline combining POS templates, n-gram LMs, CMU pronunciations, and explicit heuristics with implementation details provided.
Behavioral evaluation that measures short-term recall, one-week recognition, and subjective preference, directly addressing memorability claims.
Concrete illustrative outputs (8-digit example and 50-digit π encoding) that make the encoder's practical behavior and failure modes tangible.
limitations: No ablation experiments: the final Sentence Encoder bundles multiple heuristics (digit-weighting, POS-skipping, noun substitution, bigram post-processing) but the manuscript does not isolate which components drive encoding brevity or memorability.

Sparse quantitative characterization of outputs: aggregate metrics (mean/median words-per-digit, distribution of sentence lengths, coverage/failure rates, runtime per input) across large random samples are missing, making generalizability and practical tradeoffs unclear.

Human-study data-quality concerns: 101 of 167 initial participants were excluded for suspected fraud with qualitative criteria but without reproducible filters or sensitivity analyses; this high exclusion proportion may introduce bias in group comparisons.

Protocol deviation and test-design concerns: the intended distraction interval (~5 minutes) was not enforced (median ≈81s), and long-term memory was assessed by 5-AFC recognition using distractors generated by the same encoder family, risking cueing/familiarity effects that may inflate recognition estimates.
open_questions: Please provide exact, reproducible exclusion filters and per-participant logs (timestamps, page dwell times) and report whether primary results (short-term recall, confirmation times) hold under alternative inclusion thresholds or when borderline cases are retained.

Can the authors run ablation experiments toggling each major heuristic (remove digit-weighting, disable POS-skipping, disallow noun-for-pronoun substitution, skip bigram post-processing) and report both automatic fluency proxies (LM scores/perplexity, POS-sequence likelihood) and encoding-length statistics (words-per-digit distribution)?

How were recognition distractors generated (sampling method, similarity constraints)? Please report recognition confusion matrices and, if possible, recognition results using distractors from other encoder families or random foils and free-recall results separately.

Provide corpus-scale coverage statistics: for randomized samples of digit sequences at multiple lengths (e.g., 8, 20, 50 digits), what fraction of inputs produce encodings under specified length thresholds, how often must templates be resampled or POS slots skipped, and what are typical runtimes per input?
consensus_snapshot: Engineered Sentence Encoder is a coherent, implementable synthesis that can produce compact, pronounceable, sentence-like encodings of digits under the major system.
Illustrative examples and reported study results are suggestive that sentence-like encodings can aid short-term memorability and subjective ease relative to an n-gram baseline.

Major methodological gaps—especially absent ablations, missing aggregate encoding metrics, high/explained exclusions, and protocol deviations—limit confidence in causal attribution and generalizability of behavioral claims.
disagreement_snapshot: Reviewers differ on how much the human-study limitations undermine the behavioral claims: some consider the short-term recall result plausibly robust but in need of replication; others judge the high exclusion rate and distraction deviation as enough to substantially lower confidence until sensitivity analyses/replication are provided.

Some reviewers emphasize the approach as a meaningful incremental engineering contribution, while a subset frames it as a potentially disruptive framing if validated; this reflects differing weightings of novelty vs. required empirical rigor.
uncertainty_snapshot: Uncertainty about which heuristics (if any single one) produce the observed memorability gains due to lack of ablation.
Uncertainty about the magnitude and robustness of behavioral effects due to large participant exclusions and non-enforced distraction timing.
Uncertainty about long-term memory inference because recognition tests may be cue-biased and free-recall did not show parallel improvements.

Examples and a user study suggest potential memorability benefits versus an n-gram baseline.
Strengths: Clear engineering description and reproducible pipeline; direct behavioral evaluation (short-term recall, one-week recognition, subjective preference); concrete illustrative outputs demonstrating feasibility and compact encodings.

(2) Missing aggregate encoding statistics (words-per-digit, coverage/failure rates, runtime) across many inputs. Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

Two principle processes underlying fluency gains are knowledge compilation (e.g., Anderson & Lebiere, 1998) and memory strengthening (e.g., Logan, 1988).
